Boundary matrix of a lat/long raster, in geodesic metres

Source: R/boundary.R
geodesic_boundary_matrix.Rd

Builds the boundary matrix of a raster in geographic coordinates (longitude and latitude), with lengths in metres along the WGS84 ellipsoid. A boundary matrix holds the length of the edge shared by each pair of neighbouring planning units, as used for boundary penalties and connectivity in prioritizr and Where To Work. Use it in place of prioritizr::boundary_matrix() for a lat/long raster: prioritizr::boundary_matrix() takes a raster cell's resolution as its edge length, which is in degrees for a lat/long raster, and treats every cell as the same size. For a projected raster, or for polygons (whose lengths prioritizr already measures in geodesic metres when they are lat/long), use prioritizr::boundary_matrix().

Usage

geodesic_boundary_matrix(x)

Arguments

x

The raster: a SpatRaster in a geographic (lat/long) CRS, or a path to such a raster file. It may have several layers; a cell is a planning unit if it has a value in at least one of them.

Value

A symmetric sparse matrix (Matrix::dsCMatrix) with one row and one column per raster cell (terra::ncell(x)), in terra's cell order (row by row from the top-left cell). Off the diagonal: the length in metres of the edge two planning units share, 0 if they share none. On the diagonal: each planning unit's perimeter in metres, 0 for cells that are not planning units. A raster with no values gives a matrix of zeros. Nothing is written.

Method

  • Planning units: the cells that are not NA in at least one layer (as in prioritizr::boundary_matrix()). Cells that are NA in every layer have no edges and a perimeter of 0.

  • Edge lengths: the geodesic distance on the WGS84 ellipsoid between the two corners of each cell edge, from terra::distance() with lonlat = TRUE (the calculation terra::perim() uses for lat/long polygons). A cell's top and bottom edges are geodesics between corners at the same latitude, its side edges are meridian arcs. Every cell in a raster row has the same edge lengths, so they are computed once per row. Edge latitudes beyond the poles are set to 90 or -90 degrees.

  • Neighbours: two planning units are neighbours if they share an edge: left and right, or above and below (rook's case, not diagonal). Left and right neighbours share the side edge of their row; above and below neighbours share the bottom edge of the upper cell. On a raster that spans 360 degrees of longitude, terra treats the first and last cells of each row as left and right neighbours, sharing an edge on the antimeridian; prioritizr::boundary_matrix() on the cells as polygons does not.

  • Diagonal: each planning unit's total perimeter (top + bottom + two sides), whether or not its edges are shared, as in prioritizr::boundary_matrix().

  • Units: metres. Cell values are not used, only whether they are NA. The raster is not reprojected.

The lengths match prioritizr::boundary_matrix() on the cells as polygons (to within 1e-6 m), without building the polygons.

See also

prioritizr::boundary_matrix() for projected rasters and for polygons.

Other raster: align_raster(), polygonize_raster(), write_raster_file(), write_rasters()

Examples

# A 2 x 3 raster of 0.25 degree cells at about 50 degrees north, with one
# cell NA
x <- terra::rast(
  nrows = 2, ncols = 3, xmin = -100, xmax = -99.25, ymin = 49.75,
  ymax = 50.25, crs = "EPSG:4326", vals = c(1, 1, NA, 1, 1, 1)
)
bm <- geodesic_boundary_matrix(x)

# Side edges are about 27.8 km, top and bottom edges about 17.9 km
round(as.matrix(bm))
#>       [,1]  [,2] [,3]  [,4]  [,5]  [,6]
#> [1,] 91370 27808    0 17924     0     0
#> [2,] 27808 91370    0     0 17924     0
#> [3,]     0     0    0     0     0     0
#> [4,] 17924     0    0 91554 27807     0
#> [5,]     0 17924    0 27807 91554 27807
#> [6,]     0     0    0     0 27807 91554
